paras: The Alamance County jail shooting was the killing of James Ray and the wounding of two other men on the night of July 19, 1920, when a Durham machine-gun company guarding three Black prisoners in the jail at Graham, North Carolina, against a threatened lynching fired into a crowd. The soldiers said a mob fired on them first; Governor Thomas W. Bickett's committee upheld them, while the county grand jury found no mob and no provocation. Black newspapers praised Bickett for saving the prisoners.

The three men were held in connection with an alleged attack on a white woman. According to the Tulsa Star, Bickett sent the company, under Captain Marion B. Fowler, with the order: "Captain Fowler, protect those prisoners at all hazards." Graham witnesses admitted the crowd at the jail on Sunday, July 18, had been threatening.

On the night of July 19 the soldiers fired into a crowd near the jail, killing Ray and wounding Willis Phillips and Clem Bradshaw. In their sworn account they had been fired on by a masked mob attacking the jail and had returned the fire. Private John Thompson, off duty in Graham, swore that at 9 o'clock he saw about fifty men, most of them armed and among them Ray and Phillips, in a poolroom near the jail and heard one say they would attack it at 9:30.

Sixty-six Alamance citizens swore that the militiamen fired without provocation, and witnesses said no masked mob had formed that night. Captain Jim Smith, who lived near the jail, testified that the first shot was a faint one from a cheap pistol, not an army automatic.

Bickett's court of inquiry (A. H. Boyden, B. S. Royster and W. H. Whedbee) heard the soldiers at Durham on August 2 and citizens at Graham on August 3. On August 20 it reported that the soldiers were justified "in returning the fire, when the sentinels and jail were fired upon," and that Ray, Phillips and Bradshaw seemed to have been "innocent or curious onlookers." At the close of the August court term the Alamance grand jury found that Ray died from the machine gunners' shots, that there was no mob at the jail and that there was no provocation. No report of charges against any soldier or member of the crowd appears in the coverage.
On August 25 a mob took John Jeffress, a Black prisoner, from the sheriff at Graham and shot him near where Ray had fallen.

White papers from Richmond and Washington to Pensacola and New York carried Associated Press dispatches. Headlines followed the soldiers' defense and the committee's finding, from "Machine Gunners Defend Action in Firing Into Crowd" to the New York Sun and Herald's "Riot Killings Justified," while texts often called the attack "alleged." The High Point Review reported that observers called the gunners' evidence "well nigh impregnable," and the Roanoke Rapids Herald printed Durham Mayor Newsom's pledge of support. The Berea, Kentucky, Citizen wrote that Bickett had "saved three Negroes" and added, "Good for North Carolina!"

Black weeklies treated the episode as proof that a governor could stop a lynching. The Colorado Statesman called the dead man a "lyncher" and ranked Bickett with Governor Morrow of Kentucky, and the Tulsa Star set Bickett's order against the burning of two Black men at Paris, Texas. The Chicago Whip and the Black Dispatch printed short items on the committee's finding and the rescue.

The Raleigh Independent backed the commission against Alamance testimony that it said seemed to have "evolved out of resentment against citizen-soldiers who merely did their duty," and, after reporting the grand jury's finding, commented that "There is something essentially wrong with Alamance's sense of duty or Fair Play." After the Jeffress lynching, the Chicago Whip ran as "The Week's Worst Editorial" a white editorial calling the charge against the three prisoners "the usual heinous crime," and the Dallas Express called the new lynching "Revenge For Former Failure."

The night was given as Sunday, July 19, in one Associated Press text and Monday in others, and one printing of the committee report read "July 10." The Chicago Whip said the accusation concerned a white man; other papers said a white woman.

reader.title: Alamance County jail shooting
bases: Troops guarding three Black prisoners against an alleged mob attempt to lynch them fired into a crowd at the Graham jail, killing James Ray [A2][A21]; it is an attempted lynching, with the attack itself contested [A11][A38].

No prisoner was taken or killed [A17][A34]; the only death, James Ray, was caused by National Guard troops acting on the governor's orders [A2][A21], and whether a mob attacked at all is contested [A11][A38].

Many independent reports agree that troops guarding three Black prisoners killed Ray and wounded two [A2][A21][A17], but the alleged mob attack is affirmed by the soldiers and committee [A2][A21] and denied by citizens and the grand jury [A11][A38].

accounts.label: Soldiers' sworn testimony
accounts.gist: A masked mob fired on the sentinels and attacked the jail at about 9:30; the soldiers returned the fire; Thompson saw about fifty armed men, including Ray, planning the attack.

accounts.label: Alamance citizens' sworn statement and witnesses
accounts.gist: The militiamen fired without provocation; no masked mob formed and there was no sign of a mob at the jail, though the crowd on July 18 was threatening.

accounts.label: Governor's committee report
accounts.gist: The soldiers were justified in returning the fire when the sentinels and jail were fired upon; Ray and the wounded were not members of any organized mob but onlookers.

accounts.label: Alamance grand jury
accounts.gist: Ray died from the gunners' shots; there was no mob at the jail and no provocation.

accounts.label: Black editorials
accounts.gist: A mob rushed the jail to lynch three prisoners and was turned back by the governor's troops, who killed one and wounded one or two.

framing.detail: AP texts headlined 'Machine Gunners Defend Action in Firing Into Crowd' and 'Justify Soldiers' Action in Firing in Carolina Mob', calling the attack 'alleged'.
Sun and New York Herald headed the committee report 'Riot Killings Justified'.
High Point Review reported the gunners' case as a chain of evidence observers called 'well nigh impregnable'.
Roanoke Rapids Herald printed Mayor Newsom's support for the company under 'Durham Backs Its Military'.
Berea Citizen praised Bickett for saving three Negroes from the mob: 'Good for North Carolina!'
Colorado Statesman, 'North Carolina to the Front', called the dead man a 'lyncher' and praised Bickett.
Tulsa Star quoted Bickett's order as worthy of the nation's famous epigrams and contrasted Paris, Texas.
Chicago Whip ('O. K. Military Action') and Black Dispatch ('One Killed by Jail Guards') ran brief reports.
Raleigh Independent backed the commission and said the grand jury finding showed something 'essentially wrong with Alamance's sense of duty or Fair Play'.
Chicago Whip reprinted a white editorial on the Graham events as 'The Week's Worst Editorial'.
